html:
Semantic memory can be conceived as a vast network of concepts (nodes) connected by associations (edges), and analyses show it has a pronounced small-world topology 1. In a small-world network, most concepts are not directly connected, yet any concept can be reached from any other via only a few steps through the network. In practical terms, semantic knowledge is organized into densely interlinked clusters of related concepts (e.g. animals, tools, emotions) with short-cut links bridging across clusters via more universal or polysemous concepts 1. This architecture yields high local clustering (concepts within a category share many interconnections) alongside short global path lengths (even concepts from very different domains can be connected through surprisingly few associative hops). Such a small-world arrangement is thought to balance specialized processing with efficient integration: closely related ideas form substructures that promote context-specific priming and inference, while the overall network remains globally integrated, enabling far-flung analogies and fast knowledge transfer across domains 2. these network properties appear to be an intrinsic feature of semantic organization: studies have found small-world characteristics in semantic networks built from diverse sources (word association norms, thesauri, WordNet) and across languages, suggesting a universal architectural principle for how human knowledge is structured 3. A 2025 study illustrates network organizations (Figure) 12.

Alongside small-world clustering, semantic networks exhibit a heavy-tailed (approximately scale-free) degree distribution, meaning a minority of nodes serve as highly connected hubs linking many concepts, while most nodes have fewer connections 1, 4. In essence, some ideas (often very abstract or general ones, like "time," "person," or "move") act as major hubs with disproportionate connectivity, whereas more specific concepts are richly interlinked with their close kin but sparsely connected outside their niche. Graph-theoretically, this yields a network with hub nodes that greatly reduce the degrees of separation between any two concepts. These hubs form part of a high-connectivity backbone or "rich club" that promotes global integration: they tend to be interconnected with each other as well, creating a core subnetwork through which much information flow passes 5. In the brain’s semantic system, this graph structure is mirrored by transmodal integration hubs like the anterior temporal lobes, angular gyrus, and medial prefrontal cortex. Connectome analyses show that heteromodal default-mode regions (including key semantic areas) often rank among the most globally connected and central nodes in the whole-brain network 2. This hub architecture confers efficiency and robustness: it ensures any two distant cortical regions (or concepts) can communicate quickly via hub-mediated shortcuts, and it economizes wiring by funneling information through central highways. However, it also implies a vulnerability to hub disruption. Just as removing a highly connected node in a scale-free graph can fragment the network, damage to semantic hub regions or their white-matter connections (for example, bilateral ATL degeneration in semantic dementia) produces disproportionate deficits, effectively disconnecting many modality-specific "spoke" areas and collapsing conceptual coherence across domains 6. By contrast, damage to a peripheral spoke or a single category tends to have more circumscribed effects. Thus, the graph-theoretic lens helps explain why focal hub lesions yield generalized semantic impairments while leaving other cognitive functions intact - the network’s high-degree nodes are singularly important for holding the knowledge web together. The authors test the shape of degree distributions (Figure).

The semantic network shows modular structure with community organization aligning to meaningful subdomains. Graph analysis reveals that concepts naturally cluster into communities corresponding to thematic or categorical groupings (e.g. living things vs. artifacts, social concepts, spatial navigation concepts, etc.) 2. These modules can be thought of as the cognitive equivalent of "neighborhoods" in the semantic graph - sets of nodes with dense internal connections and shared contextual features. For instance, tools and manipulable objects form a tightly knit subnetwork linked by shared action and shape attributes, whereas social concepts cluster via person-related knowledge, and spatial landmarks via scene and place associations. This community structure is consistent with the domain-biased subnetworks observed in neuroimaging (e.g. a tool-use network, a social reasoning network, a spatial navigation network) and with classic category-specific semantic effects (such as selective impairments for living vs. nonliving things in some brain injuries); however, these communities are not isolated islands: the hub nodes (both certain high-level concepts and integrative cortical regions) serve as bridges between modules, allowing information from one domain to inform another. For example, the concept "restaurant" might link a social script module (people, roles, intentions) with an object module (food items, tools like utensils) and a spatial module (the layout of a dining area). Such cross-talk is enabled by the network’s long-range connections (edges that link nodes in different communities) and by hub regions that anatomically connect to multiple specialized areas; graph-theoretic measures of modularity and connectivity thus map neatly onto cognitive structure: high modularity underlies distinct conceptual realms, while inter-module links and low characteristic path lengths underlie our ability to combine concepts across realms (e.g. to apply social knowledge to a tool-use scenario or blend metaphors between unrelated domains). A 2026 review illustrates several network architectures (Figure) 13.

The topological properties of the semantic network have direct consequences for how we retrieve and generate knowledge. Spreading activation in a small-world, hub-supported network can quickly reach remote nodes, accounting for how a single cue can trigger far-ranging associations or creative insights. At the same time, the clustering of related concepts means that memory search tends to yield groups of similar items - a phenomenon well documented in verbal fluency tasks. When people list as many exemplars of a category as possible ("name all the animals you can"), they naturally produce items in clusters (e.g. a streak of farm animals, then a bunch of ocean creatures) and occasionally make sudden switches to a new cluster 7. Graph-theoretic models explain this as a byproduct of network topology: because related concepts are tightly interconnected, an initial probe (say, "cow") activates its neighbors ("horse," "pig," "goat"), leading to a local run of farm animals; but to avoid repetition or diminishing returns, the search process must then jump along a weaker link to a different region of the network (from "farm" cluster to "sea creatures" cluster, for example). This "semantic foraging" strategy - exploit locally, then explore globally - can emerge even from a random walk on a small-world semantic graph, and it closely resembles optimal foraging in physical space. In cognitive terms, the network’s structure itself affords an efficient search: high clustering yields rich local neighborhoods that can be thoroughly mined for related ideas, while short path lengths and hubs allow relatively effortless leaps to new contexts when needed. This helps resolve the puzzle of how human memory retrieval is both focused (sticking to a context for a time) and flexible (able to shift context and find distant associations) without an exhaustive, serial scan of our entire knowledge store. A 2026 review illustrates a cognitive association network (Figure).

Functional brain studies show that task demands can transiently shift network topology: for instance, under high semantic workload or when making unusual associations, the brain’s connectivity may become less segregated and more integrated (reducing modularity and increasing long-range communication), effectively flexing along the spectrum from localized to distributed processing. Such dynamic reconfiguration aligns with the idea of a "flexible semantic workspace" that can globally broadcast conceptual information when required (engaging a broad default-mode/semantic network), or conversely, tighten into context-specific loops for automatic retrieval of well-known facts. Pathological states also illustrate the graph dynamics: in Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias, progressive loss of associative links and node degradation leads to a less small-world-like network (more random or lattice-like), which corresponds to patients’ slowed retrieval and impoverished clustering.

Schemas and task representations can be viewed as mesoscale motifs embedded in the semantic graph. A schema effectively "adds" structured shortcut edges among otherwise distant communities (roles, objects, places, causal relations), reducing path length and increasing local clustering around event- or script-nodes (e.g., "restaurant") so that inference can proceed with minimal search. vmPFC/mPFC appears to index and reinstate these templates, biasing traversal toward schema-consistent subgraphs and coupling with hippocampus during encoding and post-encoding rest; when vmPFC is damaged, people over-accept schema-consistent lures and fail to apply the appropriate script, consistent with degraded control over which subgraph is activated 8, 9, 10, 11. In this graph-theoretic framing, semantic control networks select and transiently reconfigure subgraphs to meet task goals, while schemas provide pre-wired "network macros" that compress search and enable one-shot assimilation of consistent information.
